finding: The live range is too low at both ends, and its top is clearly too low for California-emissions (CARB) states. Only the truck class could be totalled (parts + hours x $120-$160/hr): $824-$1,697 per converter with a federal aftermarket or OEM part, and about $2,576-$2,836 with the CARB-compliant aftermarket part. No stated labor time was found for the Corolla, Camry or BMW examples, so their hours are null and no totals are given; their parts alone run $959-$1,853 (Corolla; CARB part $1,909), $622-$1,352 (Camry; CARB part $1,172; OEM manifold converter $490 list) and $397-$1,551 (BMW). So a $480 total is only reachable with the cheapest federal-only part on a few vehicles, and CARB-legal parts alone can exceed the $2,450 top before any labor. Benchmarks sit higher than the live range too: RepairPal averages $2,293-$2,468 (Camry $1,872-$1,950), AAA gives $1,000-$4,000 and ConsumerAffairs sampled $933-$4,414. Evidence points to roughly $800-$3,000 per converter for federal-emissions vehicles and up to about $4,000 where a CARB-compliant or dealer part is required. Caveats: the truck labor times are Ford's times for 2022-2023 F-150 5.0L, not the 2016 example year; several retailer pages did not state converter position; Corolla has only one priced federal aftermarket listing.
extras: Quotes often add oxygen or air-fuel sensors (frequently replaced or seized during removal), new gaskets, studs, nuts and clamps, a diagnosis fee for the catalyst-efficiency code, shop supplies and sales tax. Vehicles with two or more converters may need more than one. In California and other CARB states only CARB-compliant or OEM converters are legal, which can double the parts price; federal-only parts cannot be installed there. A converter usually fails for a reason (misfire, oil or coolant burning), so repairs to the root cause may be quoted too. A failed original converter may still be covered by the federal emissions warranty (8 years / 80,000 miles), and theft replacement may be an insurance claim.
